html:
The Buyids were a Shia dynasty from Daylam, the mountains south of the Caspian Sea, who ruled most of Iran and Iraq from 934 to 1062.

Three brothers, sons of a fisherman named Buya, rose as soldiers and seized western Iran. In 945 one of them entered Baghdad. From then on the Abbasid caliphs kept their title but obeyed Buyid emirs. Their strongest ruler, Adud al-Dawla, united the family's lands from his capital at Shiraz and built hospitals and dams. Persian culture flourished in this time of Iranian dynasties, sometimes called the Iranian Intermezzo.

The family soon split among rival princes. The Ghaznavids took their eastern lands, and the Seljuks entered Baghdad in 1055. The 1000 map places this shape in Makran and Balochistan, at the far eastern edge of the Buyid world; how firmly they ruled there is unclear. See also Buwayhid emirates.
sum: The Buyids were a Shia dynasty from Daylam, the mountains south of the Caspian Sea, who ruled most of Iran and Iraq from 934 to 1062.
